summary: Belgium is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa applied for through a Belgian embassy or visa center.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air or sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, including trams and fries stands. A little cash is occasionally useful at small markets.

safety.text: Belgium is safe overall. The main risks for visitors are pickpocketing and bag theft around Brussels' major stations (Midi/Zuid, Nord) and on busy public transport, plus occasional demonstrations in the capital.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Belgium travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September bring mild weather for city walking in Brussels, Bruges and Ghent; December is atmospheric for Christmas markets, though gray and cold.

idp.text: Belgium is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Belgium is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Belgium yet.

tips.text: Keep valuables zipped away around Brussels-Midi and Brussels-Nord stations and on the metro — pickpocketing and luggage theft are the most common tourist crimes.
The 90-day visa-free limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Belgium — days spent in France or the Netherlands draw on the same allowance.
Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, apply only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site — unofficial sites charge inflated fees for the €20 authorization.

Belgium has three official languages — Dutch in Flanders, French in Wallonia, both in Brussels. Place names change with the language (Antwerpen/Anvers, Liège/Luik), which matters when reading train boards.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Belgium?
faq.answer: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa from a Belgian embassy or visa center.

faq.question: How much does a Belgium Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: €90 for adults, €45 for children aged 6–11 and free for under-6s. The fee is set EU-wide. Applications go through the Belgian mission or visa center serving your place of residence, typically via the VisaOnWeb portal.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Belgium?
faq.answer: ETIAS is the EU's travel authorization for visa-exempt visitors and is being phased in. Once mandatory, it will cost €20 (free for under-18s and over-70s) and be valid for 3 years. Check the official travel-europe.europa.eu site for the current status.

faq.question: How do I stay in Belgium longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: You need a long-stay (type D) visa or residence permit tied to a purpose such as work, study or family reunification, applied for at the Belgian mission before travel. The short-stay allowance itself cannot be extended except in exceptional circumstances.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter Belgium with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes — EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can enter with a valid national identity card instead of a passport, and can stay without a visa; registration with the commune is required for stays over 3 months.
